sources.cite: Google Cloud documentation, Database Migration Service for PostgreSQL: Promote a migration
sources.note: Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-17. Relevant text: promotion 'disconnects the destination instance from the source' and makes it 'an independent standalone primary'; before promoting, stop all writes, scripts and client connections to the source, check the replication delay metric and wait for it to reach zero or close to it; promoting earlier 'may affect destination data accuracy'; 'Database Migration Service doesn't migrate the pg_cron extension or its cron settings' (reinstall after promotion). The promote page (read 2026-11-18): promotion 'disconnects the destination instance from the source, transforms it into an independent standalone primary'; it describes no way to undo it, so the case treats promotion as final.

brief.situation: You are the database engineer at Fennick Outdoor, moving the loyalty database from a self-managed PostgreSQL server (pg-loyalty-01) to Cloud SQL with Database Migration Service (continuous migration). At 23:00 the loyalty app was stopped and its connections closed. The runbook says: wait for replication delay to reach zero, promote, switch the app. Ten minutes later the delay still sits around 40 seconds and will not reach zero. The window ends at 00:00.
handover: The fallback plan if the window is missed: restart the app on pg-loyalty-01 and try next week.
pg-loyalty-01 runs pg_cron jobs that were set up years ago.
howItWorks: The terminal shows each command's output; the diagram shows the source server and what still writes to it, the migration job and the Cloud SQL destination.
Each command takes a minute or two; the clock moves only when you act or wait.
When you close, you write the record and explain your reasoning.

writeup.question: For the record: why the delay would not reach zero, what you did before promoting, and what changed afterwards.

parts.label: Why
parts.modelAnswer: pg_stat_activity on the source showed the pg_cron scheduler updating points every minute; the app was stopped but the database still wrote, so the delay stayed around 40 seconds.

parts.label: Before promoting
parts.modelAnswer: Disabled accrue_points on the source, watched the delay reach 0, then promoted. Promoting at 40 seconds would have lost changes and left the cron job writing to the old server.

parts.label: After
parts.modelAnswer: DMS does not migrate pg_cron, so the job is re-created on Cloud SQL; the runbook now stops in-database schedulers at step 3.

diverged.headline: Close enough is not zero

scoring.modelReasoning: With the app stopped, a flat replication delay means something still writes to the source; pg_stat_activity shows the pg_cron scheduler updating points every minute. Disable that job, wait for the delay to reach zero, then promote. Promoting early loses changes and leaves the job writing to the old server; a bigger destination does not help when changes keep arriving. DMS does not migrate pg_cron, so re-create the job on Cloud SQL and fix the runbook.
